final_text: Analytics is the most common reason teams add a read replica: a production database is tuned for many small, fast OLTP transactions, and heavy dashboard queries against the primary slow the app down. Pointing the BI tool at a replica is the usual first step before a warehouse.
note: Metabase glossary (vendor reference, not a content farm): 'The single most common reason to add a replica is analytics. A production database is tuned for OLTP'; 'Run enough of those against the primary and checkout gets slow'; 'a replica is often the right first step'. Text matches.

final_text: GDPR's data-minimisation principle (Article 5(1)(c)) requires personal data to be 'adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary' for the purpose. Analytics copies often drop or mask PII columns for this reason.
note: gdpr-info.eu Art. 5(1)(c): 'adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation)'. Quote verbatim. The 'analytics copies often drop or mask PII' sentence is a reasonable practical inference, not from the source.

final_text: Apache Iceberg is a table format for huge analytic tables, not a database: engines such as Spark, Trino, Flink, Presto and Hive read and write the same Iceberg tables and provide the SQL.
note: iceberg.apache.org: 'Iceberg is a high-performance format for huge analytic tables ... making it possible for engines like Spark, Trino, Flink, Presto, Hive and Impala to safely work with the same tables'. Text matches.

final_text: Amazon Redshift is based on PostgreSQL but stores data in columns and omits OLTP features such as secondary indexes and efficient single-row updates, so its SQL differs from PostgreSQL in places.
note: AWS Redshift dev guide: 'Amazon Redshift is based on PostgreSQL'; 'Amazon Redshift stores data in columns'; 'secondary indexes and efficient single-row data manipulation operations, have been omitted'. Text matches.

final_text: MongoDB's SQL Interface (Atlas and Enterprise Advanced) gives BI tools live, read-only access over JDBC/ODBC using MongoSQL, a SQL-92-compatible dialect that can flatten nested objects and unwind arrays. The older BI Connector reached end-of-life in September 2026 (checked October 2026).
note: MongoDB SQL Interface docs: 'live, read-only access over standard ODBC and JDBC connections'; 'MongoSQL dialect, which is SQL-92 compatible'; 'flattening nested objects and unwinding arrays'; 'The BI Connector reaches End-of-Life (EOL) in September 2026'. As of 2026-10-13 that date has passed, so 'reached' is right.

final_text: Martin Fowler names the two styles: an 'Event Notification' often carries just an id and a link back to the sender, so receivers call the source for details; 'Event-Carried State Transfer' puts the changed data in the event so receivers don't need to contact the source to do further work.
note: martinfowler.com (7 Feb 2017): Event Notification 'need not carry much data on it, often just some id information and a link back to the sender that can be queried'; Event-Carried State Transfer updates clients 'in such a way that they don't need to contact the source system in order to do further work'. Original said 'never need to call the source', which is stronger than Fowler; reworded to his wording.

final_text: Kafka caps record batch size by default at about 1 MB (broker setting message.max.bytes, default 1048588 bytes, as of Kafka 4.3), so very large full-object events need config changes or a different design.
note: kafka.apache.org/43 broker configs: message.max.bytes 'The largest record batch size allowed by Kafka (after compression if compression is enabled)', Default: 1048588. Kafka 4.3.1 (25 June 2026) is still the latest supported release per the downloads page.

final_text: Writing to the service database and then publishing to Kafka is a 'dual write': there is no shared transaction across both, so the row can be saved without the event being sent, or the event sent without the row. The transactional outbox pattern stores the message in the same database transaction and relays it to the broker later.
note: Debezium outbox blog (2019): 'we cannot have one shared transaction that would span the service's database as well as Apache Kafka'. microservices.io: 2PC across DB and broker 'is not an option'; the outbox stores messages in the DB and a 'Message relay - sends the messages stored in the outbox to the message broker'. Text matches.

final_text: Query-based (polling) CDC needs a column like LAST_UPDATE_TIMESTAMP on every table. It cannot see rows deleted since the last poll and misses intermediate updates between polls. Log-based CDC captures all of these.
note: Debezium blog (2018): 'all the captured tables need to have some column like LAST_UPDATE_TIMESTAMP'; 'polling will not allow you to identify any records that have been deleted since the last poll'; 'you might miss intermediary data changes that happen between two runs of the poll loop'. Text matches.

final_text: MongoDB does expose its changes: Debezium's MongoDB connector delegates oplog capture to MongoDB change streams. This needs a replica set or sharded cluster. A standalone server has no oplog, but a one-member replica set works.
note: Debezium MongoDB connector (stable 3.x): 'the connector does not read the oplog directly. Instead, it delegates the capture and decoding of oplog data to the' change streams feature; 'not capable of monitoring the changes of a standalone MongoDB server, since standalone servers do not have an oplog. The connector will work if the standalone server is converted to a replica set with one member.' Text matches.

final_text: A PostgreSQL replication slot keeps all WAL its consumer still needs, even while the CDC tool is down. That is how it can resume, but an abandoned slot can fill pg_wal. max_slot_wal_keep_size caps this, and unused slots should be dropped.
note: PG logical decoding: slots 'will prevent removal of required resources even when there is no connection using them ... if a slot is no longer required it should be dropped.' PG warm-standby: slots can 'retain so many WAL segments that they fill up the space allocated for pg_wal. max_slot_wal_keep_size can be used to limit the size'. Text matches.

final_text: MySQL purges binlogs after a retention period. If a Debezium connector restarts after its position was purged, it fails with an error that a new snapshot is needed; snapshot.mode=when_needed makes it re-snapshot automatically.
note: Debezium MySQL connector: 'MySQL is typically set up to purge binlogs after a specified period of time'; when the recorded position is gone the connector 'returns an error that indicates that a new snapshot is required. To configure the connector to automatically initiate a snapshot in this situation, set the value of the snapshot.mode property to when_needed'. Text matches.

final_text: Logs do not hold the full history, so CDC tools start with an initial snapshot (a full SELECT of each table) and then stream changes from the log position recorded at that point. Debezium does this on first start, and so does Airbyte's first CDC sync.
note: Debezium MySQL: 'When a Debezium MySQL connector is first started, it performs an initial consistent snapshot ... reads the binlog from the point at which the snapshot was made.' Airbyte CDC: 'The first time the sync is run, a snapshot of the current state of the data will be taken. This snapshot is created with a SELECT statement'. Text matches.

final_text: The outbox pattern combines the two approaches. The service writes an event row to an 'outbox' table in the same transaction as its business data, and CDC (e.g. Debezium) tails the log and publishes those rows to Kafka. You get application-context events without the dual-write risk.
note: Debezium outbox blog: by only modifying the source service's own database 'it avoids any potential inconsistencies of altering multiple resources at the same time'; Debezium tails the outbox table and routes events to Kafka (Outbox Event Router SMT since Sept 2019). Overlaps A-E-08 (different item, both fine).

final_text: PostgreSQL 15 and earlier allow logical replication slots only on the primary. From PostgreSQL 16 a slot can be created on a standby (set hot_standby_feedback), and PostgreSQL 17 adds failover-enabled slots so Debezium can continue after promotion.
note: Debezium PostgreSQL connector: 'PostgreSQL 15 or earlier ... you can configure logical replication slots only on the primary server'; 'PostgreSQL 16 or later ... you can set up logical replication slots on replica servers'; failover slots need 'PostgreSQL 17 or later' and 'enable Debezium to continue reading changes from a new primary server after a failover'. PG docs: hot_standby_feedback 'should be set on the standby'. Text matches.

final_text: On MySQL, a replica writes changes it receives from its source into its own binlog only when log_replica_updates is enabled. It is enabled by default in MySQL 8.4 unless binary logging is turned off, and CDC needs it to read from that replica.
note: MySQL 8.4 replication-options-binary-log (opened with WebFetch; direct download returned 403): log_replica_updates Default ON; 'enabled by default, unless you specify --skip-log-bin to disable binary logging'. Text matches.

final_text: Checkpointing prevents loss but not duplicates. Debezium says that after a crash consumers see every event 'at least once', and PostgreSQL may resend recent changes after a server crash. Sinks should apply changes idempotently, e.g. upsert by primary key.
note: Debezium FAQ: after a crash 'the application sees every event at least once'. PG logical decoding: 'in the case of a crash the slot might return to an earlier LSN, which will then cause recent changes to be sent again when the server restarts'. Text matches; upsert advice is standard practice.

final_text: CDC emits one event per changed row, not per transaction. Debezium can add BEGIN/END transaction boundary events and transaction IDs if provide.transaction.metadata is set to true (default false). Consumers can use these to regroup a transaction.
note: Debezium PostgreSQL: provide.transaction.metadata default 'false'; 'Determines whether the connector generates events with transaction boundaries and enriches change event envelopes with transaction metadata'. Text matches.

final_text: Airbyte does not treat CDC sources as infinite streams: each scheduled sync reads the log from the last saved position up to the sync's start, so a change can wait up to one sync interval (plus sync time) to arrive, and syncs must run often enough to read the logs before they are purged.
note: Airbyte CDC docs: 'We do not treat CDC sources as infinite streaming sources'; 'We read data from the previously synced position in the logs up to the start time of the sync'; 'ensure that your schedule ... is frequent enough to consume the logs'. 'Lag is at least the sync interval' is wrong: a change made just before a sync arrives quickly. Reworded to 'up to'.

final_text: In PostgreSQL 'only one receiver may consume changes from a slot at any given time'; each independent consumer needs its own slot. Debezium's PostgreSQL connector 'always uses a single task'.
note: PG logical decoding: 'Only one receiver may consume changes from a slot at any given time.' Debezium PostgreSQL tasks.max: 'The PostgreSQL connector always uses a single task'. Quotes verbatim. Largely repeats the L-0343 note, hence optional.

final_text: Redshift's built-in way to export to S3 is UNLOAD, which writes query results as text, CSV, JSON or Parquet files. By default it writes in parallel, one or more files per slice.
note: AWS UNLOAD: 'Unloads the result of a query to one or more text, JSON, or Apache Parquet files on Amazon S3'; FORMAT accepts CSV | PARQUET | JSON; 'By default, UNLOAD writes one or more files per slice.' Text matches.

final_text: MySQL caches a transaction's changes until COMMIT and then writes the whole transaction to the binary log before the commit completes, so the binlog is in commit order. The binlog exists for replication and point-in-time recovery, which is why CDC tools read it.
note: MySQL 8.4 binary-log page (via WebFetch): updates are 'cached until a COMMIT statement is received by the server. At that point, mysqld writes the entire transaction to the binary log before the COMMIT is executed'; 'This ensures that the log is logged in commit order'; purposes are replication and point-in-time recovery. The cited page does not discuss the InnoDB redo log, so that clause is replaced by what the page says.

final_text: Airbyte CDC limits: most sources support CDC only on tables with a primary key, views are not supported, and only INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE are captured (TRUNCATE and ALTER do not appear). After adding a new table you must refresh the connection so it is snapshotted before CDC tracks it.
note: Airbyte CDC 'Limitations': 'only supported for tables with primary keys for most sources'; 'Data must be in tables, not views'; 'changes made from TRUNCATE / ALTER won't appear'; 'A refresh is required after any new table/collection is added'. Reworded 'snapshot' to the doc's 'refresh'.

final_text: With Debezium on Kafka Connect, fan-out is cheap: the source is read once into Kafka topics, and separate sink connectors stream those topics to Elasticsearch, a warehouse, and so on. An Airbyte connection links one source to one destination.
note: Debezium architecture: 'Sink connectors that propagate records from Kafka topics to other systems'; records can be streamed to 'Elasticsearch, data warehouses and analytics systems'. Airbyte core concepts: a connection 'links a configured source ... to a configured destination'. Text matches.

final_text: In current Redis source the object header (redisObject) packs a 4-bit type, a 4-bit encoding, a 23-bit refcount, a few flag/metadata bits and a 24-bit lru field (LRU_BITS = 24) next to the pointer to the value. Under LFU the same 24 bits hold a 16-bit access time and an 8-bit frequency counter.
note: Opened redis/unstable src/object.h (Oct 2026). Current struct: 'unsigned type:4; unsigned encoding:4; unsigned refcount : OBJ_REFCOUNT_BITS; unsigned iskvobj : 1; unsigned metabits :8; unsigned lru:LRU_BITS; void *ptr;' with LRU_BITS 24 and OBJ_REFCOUNT_BITS 23; comment: 'LFU data (least significant 8 bits frequency and most significant 16 bits access time)'. The original's field order (lru before refcount) is the older layout; reworded without order claims.

final_text: Redis approximates LRU. At eviction time it samples a few keys (maxmemory-samples, default 5), evicts the one idle longest, and since Redis 3.0 keeps a pool of good candidates. With 10 samples the result is very close to true LRU.
note: Redis eviction docs: 'samples a small number of keys at random and then evicts the ones with the longest time since last access'; 'From Redis 3.0 onwards, the algorithm also tracks a pool of good candidates'; 'maxmemory-samples 5'; 'Using a sample size of 10 in Redis 3.0 the approximation is very close to the theoretical performance'. redis.conf: '# maxmemory-samples 5'. Text matches.

final_text: Redis LFU uses a probabilistic logarithmic (Morris) counter that saturates around one million hits and decays over time. lfu-log-factor (default 10) and lfu-decay-time (default 1 minute) tune it.
note: Redis eviction docs: 'a probabilistic counter, called a Morris counter'; defaults 'Saturate the counter at, around, one million requests' and 'Decay the counter every one minute'; 'lfu-log-factor 10 lfu-decay-time 1'. evict.c confirms the 8-bit LOG_C. Text matches.

final_text: In Redis, maxmemory 0 (the default on 64-bit) means no limit. Replication and AOF buffers are not counted toward maxmemory, so leave some RAM free for them.
note: Redis eviction docs: 'Set maxmemory to zero to specify that you don't want to limit the memory ... This is the default behavior for 64-bit systems'; replication/AOF buffer memory 'is not included in the total that is compared to maxmemory'; 'set maxmemory to leave a little RAM free'. Text matches.

final_text: Redis eviction policies: noeviction, allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, allkeys-random, volatile-lru, volatile-lfu, volatile-random, volatile-ttl, and since Redis 8.6 allkeys-lrm/volatile-lrm. The volatile-* policies only consider keys with a TTL.
note: Redis eviction docs list noeviction, allkeys-lru, allkeys-lrm, allkeys-lfu, allkeys-random, volatile-lru, volatile-lrm, volatile-lfu, volatile-random, volatile-ttl; 'Starting with Redis 8.6, the Least Recently Modified (LRM) eviction policy is available'; volatile-* use keys 'that have an associated expiration (TTL)'. Text matches.

final_text: Since Redis 6.0 (2019-2020) the active expiry cycle walks the table of keys with a TTL incrementally with a cursor, 20 keys per loop, and keeps going while more than about 10% of checked keys are expired (tunable with active-expire-effort), within a CPU-time budget.
note: Opened redis/unstable src/expire.c: '#define ACTIVE_EXPIRE_CYCLE_KEYS_PER_LOOP 20', '#define ACTIVE_EXPIRE_CYCLE_ACCEPTABLE_STALE 10 /* % of stale keys after which we do extra efforts */', 'ACTIVE_EXPIRE_CYCLE_SLOW_TIME_PERC 25 /* Max % of CPU to use */', kvstoreScan over db->expires with expires_cursor. Redis 6.0 release notes (RC1, 19 Dec 2019): 'The Redis active expire cycle was rewritten ... Now the effort is tunable.' Added the version.

final_text: Redis keeps a separate index of keys that have a TTL (db->expires). The active expiry cycle scans it, and Redis docs note that setting an expire costs memory.
note: redis/unstable server.h: redisDb has 'kvstore *expires; /* Timeout of keys with a timeout set */'. Redis eviction docs: 'setting an expire value for a key costs memory'. Text matches.

final_text: HTTP/1.1 defaults to persistent connections (RFC 9112 §9.3), so one TCP connection serves many requests. Closing a TCP connection takes a FIN and an ACK in each direction.
note: RFC 9112 §9.3: 'HTTP/1.1 defaults to the use of "persistent connections", allowing multiple requests and responses to be carried over a single connection.' RFC 9293 state machine (FIN-WAIT-1/2, CLOSE-WAIT, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT): each side sends its own FIN, which is ACKed. Text matches.

final_text: A valid HTTP/1.1 request must include a Host header, and the headers end with an empty line (CRLF CRLF). A strict server answers 400 Bad Request if Host is missing.
note: RFC 9112 §3.2: 'A server MUST respond with a 400 (Bad Request) status code to any HTTP/1.1 request message that lacks a Host header field'; the header section ends with an empty line (CRLF). Text matches. Practical detail for the netcat demo, hence optional.

final_text:
RESP sends commands as arrays of length-prefixed bulk strings (e.g. *2
$4
LLEN
$6
mylist
), so it is binary-safe and fast to parse. Redis also accepts plain 'inline' commands typed in telnet, the same trick as the netcat HTTP demo.
note:
Redis protocol spec: 'RESP is binary-safe and uses prefixed length to transfer bulk data'; example 'the client sending *2
$4
LLEN
$6
mylist
'; 'Inline commands: Sometimes you may need to send a command to the Redis server but only have telnet available'. Text matches.

final_text: gRPC frames each message with a 1-byte compressed flag and a 4-byte length over HTTP/2. Message compression is only used when a grpc-encoding header is set.
note: grpc PROTOCOL-HTTP2.md: 'Length-Prefixed-Message -> Compressed-Flag Message-Length Message'; 'Compressed-Flag -> 0 / 1 ; encoded as 1 byte unsigned integer'; 'Message-Length ... encoded as 4 byte unsigned integer'; flag 1 means compressed 'using the mechanism declared by the Message-Encoding header' (grpc-encoding). Text matches.

final_text: Redis is 'mostly single threaded': commands run on one main thread, while background threads do work such as UNLINK lazy-free, and optional I/O threads handle socket reads, writes and parsing.
note: redis/unstable redis.conf THREADED I/O: 'Redis is mostly single threaded, however there are certain threaded operations such as UNLINK, slow I/O accesses and other things that are performed on side threads'; with io-threads 'we not only use threads for writes ... but also use threads for reads and protocol parsing'; disabled by default. Text matches.

final_text: In Redis Cluster a node that does not own a key's hash slot replies with a redirect such as '-MOVED 3999 127.0.0.1:6381', and the client retries at that address.
note: Redis Cluster spec 'MOVED Redirection': 'GET x -MOVED 3999 127.0.0.1:6381 The error includes the hash slot of the key (3999) and the endpoint:port of the instance that can serve the query.' Text matches.

final_text: Redis Cluster does not use a consistent-hashing ring. It maps keys to 16384 hash slots with HASH_SLOT = CRC16(key) mod 16384 and assigns slots to master nodes, moving whole slots when resharding.
note: Redis Cluster spec: 'The cluster's key space is split into 16384 slots'; 'HASH_SLOT = CRC16(key) mod 16384'; 'Each master node in a cluster handles a subset of the 16384 hash slots'; data moves 'when resharding' by moving slots. Text matches.

final_text: Amazon's Dynamo paper uses virtual nodes so that a failed node's load 'is evenly dispersed across the remaining available nodes', and a new node takes roughly equal load from each existing node.
note: Dynamo paper (SOSP 2007, allthingsdistributed.com): 'the load handled by this node is evenly dispersed across the remaining available nodes ... the newly available node accepts a roughly equivalent amount of load from each of the other available nodes.' Quote verbatim.

final_text: Cassandra's docs list the cost of many tokens per node: more neighbours per token range, a higher probability of an outage, and more repair operations. Since 3.x a deterministic allocator gives balance with far fewer tokens than the old default of 256.
note: Cassandra docs (latest): 'Every token introduces up to 2 * (RF - 1) additional neighbors'; 'The more tokens you have, the higher the probability of an outage'; 'the number of discrete repair operations ... increases'; in 2.x the default 'had to be quite high, at 256'; '3.x + a new deterministic token allocator ... requiring a much lower number of tokens'. Text matches.

final_text: In Dynamo each key is stored on N nodes: the coordinator and its N-1 clockwise successors on the ring. Cassandra's replication factor likewise counts total copies (RF=3 means three replicas).
note: Dynamo paper: 'the coordinator replicates these keys at the N-1 clockwise successor nodes in the ring'. Cassandra docs: walk the ring 'until we encounter three distinct nodes, at which point we have found all the replicas' for RF=3. Text matches.

final_text: Redis AOF is off by default (RDB snapshots are the default). With the default 'appendfsync everysec' you can lose about one second of writes; 'always' fsyncs on every write but is very slow.
note: Redis persistence docs: 'By default Redis saves snapshots of the dataset on disk ... dump.rdb'; 'appendfsync always ... Very very slow, very safe'; 'appendfsync everysec ... you may lose 1 second of data'. redis.conf (unstable): 'appendonly no', 'appendfsync everysec'. Text matches.

final_text: In BitTorrent's Kademlia DHT a node asks the nodes it knows closest to the target. They return either peers or even closer nodes, and the requester 'iteratively queries nodes that are closer' until none are closer.
note: BEP 5: the queried node responds with peers or 'the contact information of the nodes in its routing table that are closest to the infohash'; 'The original node iteratively queries nodes that are closer to the target infohash until it cannot find any closer nodes.' Quote verbatim.

final_text: Memcached keeps a doubly linked LRU list per slab class; with its lru_maintainer mode that LRU is split into HOT, WARM and COLD lists. Production caches do pay for linked-list LRU when they judge it worth it.
note: memcached doc/new_lru.txt: 'Previously: Each slab class has an independent doubly-linked list comprising its LRU'; 'Now, enabling -o lru_maintainer ... LRU's are now split between HOT, WARM, and COLD LRU's'. The page frames the plain doubly-linked list as the older mode and the split as the lru_maintainer mode; reworded to say that.

final_text: MySQL's InnoDB buffer pool makes LRU scan-resistant with midpoint insertion: new pages enter at the head of an 'old' sublist (3/8 of the pool by default) and are promoted only if accessed again.
note: MySQL 8.4 InnoDB buffer pool (via WebFetch): 'managed as a list using a variation of the LRU algorithm'; 'When InnoDB reads a page into the buffer pool, it initially inserts it at the midpoint (the head of the old sublist)'; '3/8 of the buffer pool is devoted to the old sublist'; 'Accessing a page in the old sublist makes it young'. Text matches.

final_text: InnoDB lock compatibility: if T1 holds a shared (S) lock on a row, T2 can also get S, but T2's exclusive (X) request must wait. Two transactions that both hold S and both try to update deadlock, and InnoDB rolls one back.
note: MySQL 8.4 InnoDB locking (via WebFetch): if T1 holds S on r, 'A request by T2 for an S lock can be granted immediately' and 'A request by T2 for an X lock cannot be granted immediately'. Deadlock example: two clients each hold a FOR SHARE lock, each UPDATE waits on the other, 'InnoDB rolls back the transaction that caused the deadlock' (ERROR 1213). The example uses two rows; the same-row S-to-X case follows from the compatibility rules. Text matches.

final_text: In InnoDB, a REPEATABLE READ snapshot applies to SELECT, not necessarily to UPDATE/DELETE. DML can affect rows another transaction just committed, so check the condition in the UPDATE itself (e.g. WHERE seat_free = 1).
note: MySQL 8.4 consistent read (via WebFetch): 'The snapshot of the database state applies to SELECT statements within a transaction, not necessarily to DML statements ... a DELETE or UPDATE statement issued from another concurrent REPEATABLE READ transaction could affect those just-committed rows'. Text matches.

final_text: MySQL closes non-interactive connections idle longer than wait_timeout (default 28800 seconds), so connection pools validate or refresh idle connections.
note: MySQL 8.4 server system variables (via WebFetch, offset read): wait_timeout Default 28800, 'The number of seconds the server waits for activity on a noninteractive connection before closing it.' Pool-validation sentence is standard practice.

final_text: Linux overcommits memory by default, so malloc can succeed without physical memory behind it. If the system later runs out, 'one or more processes will be killed by the OOM killer'.
note: malloc(3): 'In case it turns out that the system is out of memory, one or more processes will be killed by the OOM killer.' kernel.org overcommit accounting: mode 0 'Heuristic overcommit handling ... This is the default.' Quote verbatim.
